claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Removing the centromere from a mini-chromosome causes its retention in the mother cell rather than its loss.
claims.source: Removing the centromere of the exact same circle was shown in previous work to cause its retention in the mother cell rather than its loss (Meinema et al., 2022; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Shcheprova et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Centromeres are necessary and sufficient for chromosomes and mini chromosomes to be lost from aging mother cells.
claims.source: Therefore, centromeres are necessary and sufficient for chromosomes and mini chromosomes to be lost from aging mother cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experiments with centromeric and non-centromeric DNA circles.

claims.claim: Old mother cells lost mini-chromosomes expressing short-lived GFP at essentially the same frequency as they lost the TetO-labeled ones.
claims.source: Scoring of the GFP signal demonstrated that old mother cells lost these mini-chromosomes at essentially the same frequency as they lost the TetO-labeled one (Figure 1B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C comparing different labeling methods.

claims.claim: There was a striking increase in the frequency of chromosome missegregation in old mother cells during anaphase.
claims.source: Analysis of anaphases in old mother cells revealed a striking increase in the frequency of chromosome missegregation, using labeled chromosome II, IV, and minichromosome as reporters (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In 600 total anaphase events, 66 (11%) co-segregated the labeled sister chromatids to a single pole with 54/66 (82%) resulting in asymmetric partition to the bud.
claims.source: In 600 total anaphase events captured in our movies, we found that 66 (11%) of them co-segregated the labeled sister chromatids to a single pole with 54/66 (82%) of the missegregation events resulting in asymmetric partition of the chromatids to the bud of these old mother cells (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of anaphase events shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Asymmetric chromosome segregation to the bud was virtually never observed in young cells.
claims.source: This was virtually never observed in young cells (Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing young and old cells in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Chromosome loss from old mother cells is fully explained by a rise in sister chromatid non-disjunction with age, resulting in co-segregation of the sister chromatids asymmetrically to the bud.
claims.source: Therefore, chromosome loss from old mother cells seems fully explained by a rise in sister chromatid non-disjunction with age, resulting in co-segregation of the sister chromatids asymmetrically to the bud.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantitative agreement between chromosome loss frequency and anaphase missegregation frequency.

claims.claim: The pre-existing (old) SPB segregates in a highly biased manner to the bud (~95% of mitoses) in budding yeast.
claims.source: In budding yeast, the pre-existing (old) SPB, which the cell inherited from the previous mitosis, segregates in a highly biased manner to the bud (~95% of mitoses) (Lengefeld et al., 2017; Pereira et al., 2001; Hotz et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In about 10% of old cells, SPB inheritance is inverted, meaning that the old SPB goes to the mother cell instead of the daughter.
claims.source: In about 10% of old cells, SPB inheritance is inverted, meaning that the old SPB goes to the mother cell instead of the daughter (Lengefeld et al., 2017; Pereira et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In 80% of cases where SPB inheritance was inverted, the non-disjoining sister chromatids followed the old SPB to the mother cell instead of going to the bud.
claims.source: In a strong majority of these cases (80%), the non-disjoining sister chromatids followed the old SPB to the mother cell, instead of going to the bud (Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E analyzing SPB-chromosome co-segregation.

claims.claim: Non-disjoining sister chromatids of old mother cells remained attached to the pre-existing SPB and partitioned with it to the bud, causing them to lose these chromosomes.
claims.source: We conclude that non-disjoining sister chromatids of old mother cells remained attached to the pre-existing SPB and partitioned with it to the bud, causing them to lose these chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of SPB-chromosome co-segregation patterns.

claims.claim: In budding yeast, sister chromatids both initially attach to the pre-existing SPB, and these syntelic attachments are then dissolved by the aurora B kinase.
claims.source: In budding yeast, sister chromatids both initially attach to the pre-existing SPB, which is available first. These syntelic attachments are then dissolved by the aurora B kinase, allowing sister chromatids to reorient, reach bi-orientation, and partition symmetrically in mitosis (Biggins et al., 1999; Cheeseman et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies describing the error correction mechanism.

claims.claim: Failure to correct initial attachment errors causes sister chromatids to co-segregate with the old SPB to the bud.
claims.source: Failure to correct these initial attachment errors causes sister chromatids to co-segregate with the old SPB to the bud (Tanaka et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Young cells carrying the temperature-sensitive ipl1-321 mutant allele and grown at a permissive temperature (27 °C) showed no detectable chromosome loss.
claims.source: Young cells carrying the temperature-sensitive ipl1-321 mutant allele and grown at a permissive temperature (27 °C) showed no detectable chromosome loss (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: ipl1-321 mutant cells started losing chromosomes early in age, resulting in a shortened lifespan.
claims.source: However, they started losing chromosomes early in age (Figure 2F), resulting in a shortened lifespan (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The chromosome loss frequency of the old ipl1-321 mutant cells (t=24 h) was indistinguishable from that of the wild-type cells, indicating that the effects of age and reducing Ipl1 activity were not additive.
claims.source: Strikingly, the chromosome loss frequency of the old ipl1-321 mutant cells (t=24 h) was indistinguishable from that of the wild-type cells, indicating that the effects of age and reducing Ipl1 activity were not additive (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F comparing loss frequencies.

claims.claim: Old cells lose chromosomes due to defects in correcting chromosome attachment errors.
claims.source: We concluded that old cells lose chromosomes due to defects in correcting chromosome attachment errors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the non-additive effects of age and ipl1-321 mutation.

claims.claim: Mutant cells lacking the deacetylase Sir2 form ERCs at an increased rate, accumulate them quicker, and their replicative lifespan is shorter than that of wild-type cells.
claims.source: Mutant cells lacking the deacetylase Sir2, which inhibits recombination in the rDNA locus, form ERCs at an increased rate, accumulate them quicker, and their replicative lifespan is shorter than that of wild-type cells (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Kaeberlein et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: sir2Δ mutant cells showed a strong and premature loss of the reporter chromosome.
claims.source: Supporting the notion that ERC accumulation might promote chromosome loss, these mutant cells also showed a strong and premature loss of the reporter chromosome (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Removing replication fork barriers by inactivating the fork barrier protein Fob1 drastically decreases the rate at which ERCs form and accumulate, stabilizes the nuclear baskets of NPCs, and prolongs the life span of the cells.
claims.source: Therefore, removing these fork barriers, for example, by inactivating the fork barrier protein Fob1, drastically decreases the rate at which ERCs form and accumulate, stabilizes the nuclear baskets of NPCs, and prolongs the life span of the cells (Meinema et al., 2022; Defossez et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: fob1Δ mutant cells lost chromosome II at a substantially reduced frequency compared to wild-type cells, even after dividing 20 times or more.
claims.source: Strikingly, the fob1∆ mutant cells trapped in our microfluidics platform lost chromosome II at a substantially reduced frequency compared to wild-type cells, even after dividing 20 times or more (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Introducing an artificial replicative DNA circle with a different sequence than an ERC into wild-type cells promoted chromosome loss.
claims.source: Introducing an artificial replicative DNA circle with a different sequence than an ERC into wild-type cells also promoted chromosome loss, supporting the idea that DNA circles promote chromosome loss with age independently of their sequence (see below).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented later in the manuscript (Figure 6).

claims.claim: Chromosome loss rates correlate well with the accumulation of extrachromosomal DNA circles.
claims.source: Taken together, the chromosome loss rates seen in cells with artificial DNA circles, along with those in sir2∆ and fob1∆ cells, show that chromosome loss correlates well with the accumulation of extrachromosomal DNA circles.
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on multiple genetic manipulations affecting ERC levels.

claims.claim: Removal of the SAGA subunit Sgf73, which mediates ERC attachment to NPCs and the subsequent displacement of their nuclear basket, phenocopied the effect of the fob1Δ mutation.
claims.source: Supporting this notion, removal of the SAGA subunit Sgf73, which mediates ERC attachment to NPCs and the subsequent displacement of their nuclear basket, phenocopied the effect of the fob1∆ mutation (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014): the sgf73∆ mutant cells failed to show any significant increase in chromosome loss frequency at any age (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citation to previous work on Sgf73 function.

claims.claim: ERC formation and anchorage to NPCs triggered chromosome loss in old yeast cells.
claims.source: Thus, our data suggested that ERC formation and anchorage to NPCs triggered chromosome loss in old yeast cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic experiments with sir2Δ, fob1Δ, and sgf73Δ mutants.

claims.claim: mlp1Δ single mutant cells exhibited a rapid increase in chromosome loss frequency as they aged, along with a shortened replicative lifespan.
claims.source: In stark contrast to the sgf73∆ and fob1∆ single mutants and the wild-type cells, the mlp1∆ single mutant cells exhibited a rapid increase in chromosome loss frequency as they aged, as determined by using our reporter chromosome II, along with a shortened replicative lifespan (Figure 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claims.claim: Displacement of the basket from NPCs as the cells age promotes chromosome loss through some yet unknown mechanism.
claims.source: Thus, our data suggest that displacement of the basket from NPCs as the cells age promotes chromosome loss through some yet unknown mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mlp1Δ phenotype.

claims.claim: Only three genes involved in chromosome segregation contain an intron: NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
claims.source: While perusing the list of genes involved in chromosome segregation (Figure 4A), we noticed that only three of them contain an intron, NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the yeast genome and is presented in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 all function with Ipl1/aurora B in preventing syntelic chromosome attachment.
claims.source: Surprisingly, these three genes all function with Ipl1/aurora B in preventing syntelic chromosome attachment. Nbl1/borealin is a component of the chromosome passenger complex of which aurora B/Ipl1 is the catalytic subunit. Mcm21/CENP-O is a docking receptor for Ipl1/aurora B at kinetochores. Glc7/PP1A is the protein phosphatase 1, which counteracts aurora B by dephosphorylating its targets at the outer-kinetochore (Pinsky et al., 2006; Poddar et al., 1999; Nakajima et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies describing the functions of these proteins.

claims.claim: Removing each intron individually or all three simultaneously (3 x∆i strain) had no detectable effects on chromosome segregation in young cells.
claims.source: Removing each intron individually or all three simultaneously (3 x∆i strain) had no detectable effects on chromosome segregation in young cells (Figure 4B), cell growth and mitotic timing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C.

claims.claim: Simultaneously removing all three introns nearly completely suppressed chromosome loss in old cells.
claims.source: Simultaneously removing all three introns nearly completely suppressed chromosome loss in old cells (Figure 4B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claims.claim: Removing the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 individually or in pairs suppressed chromosome loss, albeit the effects were milder than removing all three.
claims.source: Removing them individually or in pairs did so as well, albeit the effects were milder.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The simultaneous removal of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 introns did not affect the duration of the last budding event.
claims.source: Importantly, the simultaneous removal of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 introns did not affect the duration of the last budding event (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), indicating that it suppressed chromosome loss without altering cell cycle progression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Removing the introns of the two α-tubulin genes TUB1 and TUB3 simultaneously had no effect on chromosome loss.
claims.source: Removing the introns of the two α-tubulin genes TUB1 and TUB3 simultaneously had no effect, indicating that the observed effects were specifically related to the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 and not to introns in general (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B as a negative control.

claims.claim: The effects of removing the three introns were similar for chromosome II and chromosome IV, indicating that the role of these introns was not chromosome specific.
claims.source: The effects observed were similar for chromosome II and chromosome IV, indicating that the role of these introns was not chromosome specific (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Removing the three introns also suppressed the occurrence of asymmetric anaphases in old cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, removing these three introns also suppressed the occurrence of asymmetric anaphases in old cells (Figure 4C), supporting the view that asymmetric chromosome segregation and chromosome loss go hand-in-hand and are under the control of these three introns.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Removal of the three introns also suppressed chromosome loss in the ipl1-321 mutant cells.
claims.source: Strengthening this conclusion, removal of these introns also suppressed chromosome loss in the ipl1-321 mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Simultaneous removal of MCM21, NBL1, and GLC7 introns extended replicative lifespan up to ~20%.
claims.source: Remarkably, simultaneous removal of MCM21, NBL1, and GLC7 introns also had a substantial effect on the longevity of the cells, extending their replicative lifespan up to ~20% (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: A similar lifespan extension effect was observed in the ipl1-321 mutant cells upon intron removal.
claims.source: A similar effect was observed in the ipl1-321 mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Chromosome loss may be the first direct cause of death for many yeast cells upon aging, although other mechanisms eventually take over when chromosome loss is abrogated.
claims.source: Thus, chromosome loss may indeed be the first direct cause of death for many yeast cells upon aging, although other mechanisms eventually take over when chromosome loss is abrogated.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the partial lifespan extension observed when chromosome loss is suppressed.

claims.claim: mlp1Δ mutant cells exhibited a fourfold increase in their chromosome missegregation frequency compared to young wild-type cells.
claims.source: Analysis of chromosome II segregation indicated that the mlp1∆ mutant cells not only exhibited a fourfold increase in their chromosome missegregation frequency compared to the young wild-type cells, but ~80% of these missegregation events followed the old SPB, as in old cells (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claims.claim: ~80% of chromosome missegregation events in mlp1Δ mutant cells followed the old SPB, as in old cells.
claims.source: Analysis of chromosome II segregation indicated that the mlp1∆ mutant cells not only exhibited a fourfold increase in their chromosome missegregation frequency compared to the young wild-type cells, but ~80% of these missegregation events followed the old SPB, as in old cells (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Chromosome loss in mlp1Δ mutant cells was suppressed upon removal of the introns of MCM21, NBL1, and GLC7.
claims.source: Furthermore, this chromosome loss was suppressed upon removal of the introns of MCM21, NBL1, and GLC7 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Defects in the nuclear basket result in asymmetric chromosome partitioning in an intron-dependent manner in young cells.
claims.source: Therefore, although to a lower extent than in old cells, defects in the nuclear basket result in asymmetric chromosome partitioning in an intron-dependent manner in young cells as well.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mlp1Δ phenotype and its suppression by intron removal.

claims.claim: Removal of the three introns rescued the age-dependent chromosome loss and partially restored the longevity of the mlp1Δ mutant cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, removal of these three introns also rescued the age-dependent chromosome loss and partially restored the longevity of the mlp1∆ mutant cells (Figure 5D–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claims.claim: Intron-dependent dampening of the error correction pathway is one, even if not the only progeric effects of the mlp1Δ mutation.
claims.source: We concluded that intron-dependent dampening of the error correction pathway is one, even if not the only progeric effects of the mlp1∆ mutation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the partial rescue of mlp1Δ phenotypes by intron removal.

claims.claim: Basket displacement promotes chromosome loss in young mutant cells and old wild-type mother cells.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that basket displacement promotes chromosome loss in young mutant cells and old wild-type mother cells.
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on the mlp1Δ and aging phenotypes.

claims.claim: Cells carrying YRp17 showed a much shorter lifespan (10 CBE median RLS).
claims.source: As expected (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997), the cells carrying YRp17 showed a much shorter lifespan (10 CBE median RLS, Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The effect of YRp17 on longevity was substantially suppressed by the 3 x∆i mutations.
claims.source: Remarkably, however, the effect of YRp17 on longevity was substantially suppressed by the 3 x∆i mutations (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Introducing YRp17 DNA circle promoted chromosome loss, starting early in life and increasing rapidly with age.
claims.source: Analysis of chromosome loss indicated that introducing this DNA circle promoted chromosome loss, starting early in life and increasing rapidly with age (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Removal of the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 (3 x∆i cells) largely suppressed the effect of YRp17 on chromosome loss.
claims.source: Furthermore, removal of the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7 (3 x∆i cells) largely suppressed the effect of YRp17 on chromosome loss.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The suppressive effect of the 3 x∆i mutations on longevity and chromosome loss caused by YRp17 was only partial, indicating that YRp17 promotes chromosome loss through both a mechanism that involves these three introns, and at least one additional mechanism independent of these introns.
claims.source: However, note that the suppressive effect of the 3 x∆i mutations on longevity and chromosome loss was only partial, indicating that YRp17 promotes chromosome loss through both a mechanism that involves these three introns, and at least one additional mechanism independent of these introns.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the partial suppression observed.

claims.claim: The 3 x∆i triple mutation significantly, though modestly, improved the longevity phenotype of sir2Δ mutant cells.
claims.source: Supporting this hypothesis, the 3 x∆i triple mutation significantly, though modestly, improved the longevity phenotype of these cells (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The triple intron removal ameliorated the premature chromosome loss phenotype of the sir2Δ mutant cells.
claims.source: As in cells carrying YRp17, the triple intron removal indeed ameliorated the premature chromosome loss phenotype of the sir2∆ mutant cells (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The accumulation of DNA circles promotes the dissociation of the basket from NPCs and thereby drives chromosome loss at least in part through the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
claims.source: Thus, we concluded that the accumulation of DNA circles, such as ERCs and others, which promote the dissociation of the basket from NPCs and thereby drive chromosome loss at least in part through the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis conclusion based on the YRp17 and sir2Δ experiments.

claims.claim: The effect of basket displacement on chromosome loss appeared to be the dominant one in physiologically aged cells, but additional effects seem to further promote chromosome loss in the sir2Δ mutant cells and cells carrying an exogenous DNA circle.
claims.source: While this effect appeared to be the dominant one in physiologically aged cells, additional effects seem to further promote chromosome loss in the sir2∆ mutant cells and cells carrying an exogenous DNA circle, such as YRp17.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the partial suppression by intron removal in sir2Δ and YRp17 contexts.

claims.claim: Basket mutant cells fail to retain unspliced pre-mRNAs in the nucleus.
claims.source: Since basket mutant cells fail to retain unspliced pre-mRNAs in the nucleus (Galy et al., 2004; Bonnet and Palancade, 2015), we reasoned that old yeast mother cells also might leak pre-mRNAs to the cytoplasm.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In the yeast genome, only 20 introns are longer than 500 nucleotides.
claims.source: In the yeast genome, only 20 introns are longer than 500 nucleotides.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the yeast genome structure.

claims.claim: With each of the three intron probes (DBP2, YRA1, GLC7), one or two nuclear foci were detected in young cells, and only very few cells (<3%) showed a focus in the cytoplasm.
claims.source: With each of these three series of smRNA FISH probes, we detected one or two nuclear foci in young cells (Figure 7A). Only very few cells (<3%) showed a focus in the cytoplasm.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA FISH data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claims.claim: No smRNA FISH foci were detected upon deleting the corresponding introns (∆i), demonstrating probe specificity.
claims.source: No foci were detected upon deleting the corresponding introns (∆i), demonstrating probe specificity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by control data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: For each of the three introns tested, smRNA FISH detected intronic RNA sequences in the cytoplasm of most old cells.
claims.source: In contrast, for each of the three introns tested, smRNA FISH detected intronic RNA sequences in the cytoplasm of most old cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by smRNA FISH data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claims.claim: ~70% of GLC7 smRNA FISH foci were found in the cytoplasm of old mother cells, compared to ~3% in young cells.
claims.source: For example, in the case of GLC7, ~70% of smRNA FISH foci were found in the cytoplasm of old mother cells, compared to ~3% in young cells (Figure 7A–B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: 3 out of 3 tested introns showed a strong tendency to leak to the cytoplasm in old mother cells.
claims.source: Thus, 3 out of 3 tested introns showed a strong tendency to leak to the cytoplasm in old mother cells.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the smRNA FISH results.

claims.claim: The mCherry/GFP ratio of the pre-mRNA translation reporter increased in old compared to young cells, demonstrating elevated pre-mRNA translation in the cytoplasm of a large majority of aged cells.
claims.source: Fluorescence signal analysis established that the mCherry/GFP ratio increased in old compared to young cells, demonstrating elevated pre-mRNA translation in the cytoplasm of a large majority of aged cells (Figure 7D–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D-E using the pre-mRNA translation reporter.

claims.claim: The mCherry/GFP ratio increased prematurely and to a higher level in the sir2Δ mutant, compared to the wild-type cells.
claims.source: Consistent with ERC-dependent leakage and translation of this reporter, the mCherry/GFP ratio increased prematurely and to a higher level in the sir2∆ mutant, compared to the wild-type cells (Figure 7D–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claims.claim: The fob1Δ mutant cells showed a lowered mCherry/GFP ratio, which did not increase much during their lifespan.
claims.source: Conversely, the fob1∆ mutant cells showed a lowered mCherry/GFP ratio, which did not increase much during their lifespan (Figure 7D–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claims.claim: ERC formation and accumulation promote pre-mRNA leakage during yeast aging.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that ERC formation and accumulation promote pre-mRNA leakage during yeast aging, as expected from their effect on the nuclear basket.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pre-mRNA reporter data in different genetic backgrounds.

claims.claim: The two yeast SR-proteins Gbp2 and Hrb1 have been implicated in the retention of pre-mRNAs in the nucleus by binding intron-containing transcripts and delaying their export until they are properly spliced or degraded.
claims.source: The two yeast SR-proteins Gbp2 and Hrb1 have been implicated in the retention of pre-mRNAs in the nucleus by binding intron-containing transcripts and delaying their export until they are properly spliced or degraded (Hackmann et al., 2014; Hurt et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant cells leak pre-mRNA to the cytoplasm at a higher rate than wild-type cells.
claims.source: Accordingly, the hrb1∆ gbp2∆ double mutant cells leak pre-mRNA to the cytoplasm at a higher rate than wild-type cells (Hackmann et al., 2014; Windgassen et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Young spliceosome-defective snu66Δ mutant cells exhibited a fivefold elevated level of chromosome missegregation compared to young wild-type cells.
claims.source: The young spliceosome-defective snu66∆ mutant cells did exhibit a fivefold elevated level of chromosome missegregation compared to young wild-type cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Chromosome missegregation in snu66Δ mutant cells was not biased towards any specific SPB.
claims.source: However, this missegregation was not biased towards any specific SPB (Figure 8A–B), suggesting that it involved a distinct mechanism than that observed in old cells and in young cells lacking the basket protein Mlp1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: The hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant cells showed a more than 10-fold increased frequency of chromosome missegregation compared to young wild-type cells.
claims.source: In contrast to the snu66∆ mutant, the hrb1∆ gbp2∆ double mutant cells showed an even further increased frequency of chromosome missegregation, which was more than 10-fold above that of young wild-type cells (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Sister chromatid missegregation in hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant cells was strongly biased towards the old SPB.
claims.source: Furthermore, sister chromatid missegregation was strongly biased towards the old SPB (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Removing the introns of GLC7, MCM21, and NBL1 suppressed the chromosome segregation defect in hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant cells.
claims.source: Removing the introns of GLC7, MCM21, and NBL1 suppressed this chromosome segregation defect (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Pre-mRNA leakage is sufficient to induce asymmetric chromosome partitioning and is contingent on the presence of introns in the error correction genes NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
claims.source: Therefore, pre-mRNA leakage is sufficient to induce asymmetric chromosome partitioning and is contingent on the presence of introns in the error correction genes NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the hrb1Δ gbp2Δ phenotype and its suppression by intron removal.

claims.claim: Mutations affecting the spliceosome did not promote asymmetric chromosome segregation to any specific SPB with age, indicating that the chromosome loss observed in old cells is not due to splicing defects.
claims.source: The fact that mutations affecting the spliceosome did not promote asymmetric chromosome segregation to any specific SPB with age indicates that the chromosome loss observed in old cells is not due to splicing defects.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison between snu66Δ and hrb1Δ gbp2Δ phenotypes.

claims.claim: The accumulation of extrachromosomal DNA causes the displacement of the NPC basket and subsequent leakage of pre-mRNAs.
claims.source: We conclude that the accumulation of extrachromosomal DNA causes the displacement of the NPC basket and subsequent leakage of pre-mRNAs.

results.result: Old yeast cells (18-22 CBE) lose chromosomes at a frequency of 10-15%, as demonstrated by fluorescent labeling of chromosomes II and IV. Chromosome loss is fatal to haploid cells and occurs specifically in the last division of old mother cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C32 provide converging evidence from multiple labeling methods (TetO, LacO, GFP) and chromosomes showing that young cells retain all chromosomes while 10-15% of old cells lose them. The dual-labeling experiments (C28) and lethality data (C29) confirm whole chromosome loss rather than just label loss. The quantification is consistent across different reporters (C26).

results.result: Centromeres are necessary and sufficient for chromosome loss in aging, as demonstrated by experiments showing that centromeric DNA circles are lost at similar rates to full chromosomes (~20%), while non-centromeric circles are retained.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 establish through gain-of-function (adding CEN to circles) and loss-of-function (removing CEN) experiments that centromeres drive chromosome loss. The consistency across different labeling methods (C38) strengthens this conclusion. The logic is sound and the controls are appropriate.

results.result: Chromosome loss in old cells occurs through asymmetric sister chromatid non-disjunction during anaphase, with 11% of anaphases showing co-segregation of sister chromatids to a single pole, predominantly (82%) to the bud.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 provide direct time-lapse microscopy evidence of the mechanism. The quantitative agreement between chromosome loss frequency (~10-15%) and anaphase missegregation frequency (11%) supports the conclusion that non-disjunction fully explains chromosome loss. The age-specificity (C41) is well-documented.

results.result: Non-disjoining sister chromatids co-segregate with the pre-existing (old) SPB, as shown by 80% of missegregated chromosomes following the old SPB regardless of whether it goes to the bud or mother.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 establish through SPB tracking that chromosome missegregation is linked to SPB identity rather than mother-daughter identity. The use of SPB inheritance inversions (C44-C45) as a natural experiment is elegant and provides strong evidence. The 80% co-segregation rate is statistically robust.

results.result: Old cells lose chromosomes due to defects in correcting syntelic chromosome attachments, as demonstrated by non-additive effects of aging and ipl1-321 mutation on chromosome loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 establish the mechanistic link to error correction through the ipl1-321 temperature-sensitive mutant. The non-additivity (C51) is key evidence that aging and reduced Ipl1 activity affect the same pathway. The background knowledge about syntelic attachments (C47-C48) is well-established and correctly applied.

results.result: ERC accumulation drives chromosome loss in aging, as shown by accelerated loss in sir2Δ mutants (increased ERCs) and suppressed loss in fob1Δ and sgf73Δ mutants (decreased ERCs or prevented ERC-NPC anchorage).
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C60 provide genetic evidence linking ERC levels to chromosome loss through multiple independent manipulations. The sir2Δ and fob1Δ mutations affect ERC formation rates in opposite directions with corresponding opposite effects on chromosome loss. The sgf73Δ phenocopy (C59) strengthens the conclusion that ERC anchorage to NPCs is critical.

results.result: Nuclear basket displacement promotes chromosome loss, as mlp1Δ mutant cells show rapid increase in chromosome loss frequency and shortened lifespan.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 establish that basket displacement is sufficient to cause chromosome loss through direct genetic disruption of the basket protein Mlp1. The phenotype is strong and consistent with the hypothesis, though the mechanism remains unknown at this stage (C62 acknowledges this).

results.result: Removing the introns of three genes (NBL1, MCM21, GLC7) involved in the aurora B error correction pathway nearly completely suppresses chromosome loss in old cells and extends lifespan by ~20%.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C75 provide comprehensive evidence that these three specific introns are critical. The specificity is demonstrated by: (1) these are the only intron-containing genes in the segregation machinery (C63), (2) all function with aurora B (C64), (3) tubulin intron removal has no effect (C69), (4) effects are chromosome-independent (C70), and (5) suppression works in both old cells and ipl1-321 mutants (C72). The lifespan extension (C73) validates functional significance.

results.result: Basket defects in young mlp1Δ cells cause intron-dependent asymmetric chromosome partitioning similar to old cells, with ~80% of missegregation events following the old SPB, and this is suppressed by removing the three introns.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C82 establish that basket displacement is sufficient to cause the aging phenotype in young cells. The similarity in SPB bias (C77) and suppression by intron removal (C78) strongly support a common mechanism. The partial rescue of lifespan (C80) indicates intron-dependent effects are major but not sole contributors.

results.result: Introduction of the non-centromeric replicative plasmid YRp17 promotes chromosome loss and shortens lifespan, effects that are substantially but not completely suppressed by removing the three introns.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 demonstrate that DNA circle accumulation (independent of ERCs) is sufficient to cause chromosome loss. The partial suppression by intron removal (C87) indicates both intron-dependent and intron-independent mechanisms contribute, with the former being dominant. The experimental design is sound.

results.result: The triple intron removal (3xΔi) significantly but modestly improves longevity and ameliorates chromosome loss in sir2Δ mutant cells, indicating that DNA circle accumulation drives chromosome loss partly through the three introns.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 provide additional genetic evidence linking DNA circles to intron-dependent chromosome loss. The modest effect in sir2Δ background (compared to stronger effects in wild-type aging) suggests additional mechanisms operate when ERC levels are very high. This is appropriately acknowledged in C91.

results.result: Single-molecule RNA FISH experiments show that intronic sequences from three tested introns (DBP2, YRA1, GLC7) are predominantly nuclear in young cells (<3% cytoplasmic) but leak to the cytoplasm in most old cells (~70% cytoplasmic for GLC7).
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C98 provide direct visualization evidence of pre-mRNA leakage. The specificity controls (C95) confirm probe specificity. Testing three independent introns (3/3 showing leakage, C98) strengthens the conclusion. The quantification is clear and the age-dependent change is dramatic.

results.result: A pre-mRNA translation reporter shows elevated cytoplasmic translation of unspliced transcripts in old cells, with premature increase in sir2Δ mutants and suppression in fob1Δ mutants, demonstrating ERC-dependent pre-mRNA leakage.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 provide functional evidence that leaked pre-mRNAs are translated in the cytoplasm. The genetic manipulations affecting ERC levels (C100-C101) show expected correlations, supporting the causal link between ERCs, basket displacement, and pre-mRNA leakage. The reporter design is appropriate.

results.result: Pre-mRNA leakage is sufficient to induce asymmetric chromosome partitioning, as hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutants show >10-fold increased missegregation biased toward the old SPB, which is suppressed by removing the three introns. In contrast, spliceosome defects (snu66Δ) cause unbiased missegregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C111 provide critical evidence distinguishing pre-mRNA leakage from splicing defects. The hrb1Δ gbp2Δ phenotype recapitulates the aging phenotype (SPB bias, intron-dependence), while snu66Δ does not, demonstrating that leakage rather than splicing per se causes the defect. This is a key mechanistic distinction.

results.result: The accumulation of extrachromosomal DNA causes NPC basket displacement and subsequent pre-mRNA leakage, which impairs correction of syntelic attachments by the aurora B pathway through an unknown mechanism involving the introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C115 synthesize the main mechanistic pathway established by the study. The causal chain is well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches. The acknowledgment that the precise molecular mechanism remains unknown (C115) is appropriate and honest.

results.result: NPC remodeling is both necessary and sufficient to drive age-associated chromosome loss, as interventions promoting basket displacement enhance chromosome loss while interventions preventing NPC remodeling suppress it.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 summarize the necessity and sufficiency evidence from the genetic experiments. The bidirectional manipulations (promoting and preventing NPC remodeling) with corresponding effects on chromosome loss provide strong support for causality. This is a well-justified synthesis of the results.

results.result: Despite pleiotropic effects of sir2Δ and fob1Δ mutations, DNA circle accumulation and attachment to NPCs trigger chromosome loss, as supported by the common denominator of ERC effects and the phenocopy by sgf73Δ mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C124 address potential confounders and provide logical arguments for the specificity of the ERC-NPC connection. The reasoning is sound: while individual mutations have multiple effects, their common denominator (ERC/NPC effects) and the independent confirmation by sgf73Δ support the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Chromosome loss in old cells is due to non-correction of syntelic attachments, requires the three introns of NBL1, MCM21, and GLC7, and is directly linked to basket displacement and pre-mRNA leakage. Intron removal separates aging from chromosome loss, indicating these introns are part of the proximal cause.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C135 provide a comprehensive mechanistic summary. The evidence is strong and convergent from multiple approaches. The key insight that intron removal separates aging from chromosome loss (C131) is important for establishing causality. The direct link between basket displacement and chromosome loss through pre-mRNA leakage is well-established.

results.result: Basket displacement could affect multiple cellular functions beyond chromosome segregation, including protein quality control, gene activation, and processes related to ubiquitin-mediated degradation, mitochondrial function, and ribosome assembly, as introns are enriched in genes involved in these aging-related processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C142 are largely speculative (C136, C138, C139, C142) based on known basket functions (C137) and intron distribution patterns (C140-C141). While the speculation is reasonable and well-grounded in the literature, there is no direct experimental evidence in this study supporting these broader effects. This represents interesting hypotheses for future work.

results.result: Basket displacement occurs in stressed cells (e.g., heat shock) and might represent a selected response to stress that promotes karyotype variation, potentially relevant to stress-induced aneuploidy in yeast and cancer cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C150 are largely speculative, connecting the findings to stress response and cancer biology. While the cited evidence for basket displacement during heat shock (C144) and stress-induced aneuploidy (C146-C147) is valid, the proposed evolutionary advantage (C148-C149) and relevance to cancer (C150) are speculative hypotheses without direct experimental support.

results.result: Basket displacement in aging is evolutionarily conserved, occurring in mammalian hepatocytes and upon progerin expression, and might be relevant to Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome, suggesting investigation of progerin effects on pre-mRNA leakage.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C157 extend the findings to mammalian systems based on literature evidence (C152, C153, C155). While the cited evidence for basket displacement in mammals is valid, the functional relevance to mammalian aging and progeria (C156-C157) remains speculative. The suggestion for future research is reasonable but the connection is not experimentally demonstrated.

results.result: The effect of ERCs on NPCs may explain how ERCs cause aging in yeast and connect to aging in other eukaryotes. Yeast aging might reflect a death pathway for pathogen control, analogous to inflammation in metazoans, and might have emerged as an anti-viral defense.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C164 present highly speculative evolutionary hypotheses about the origin and significance of the ERC-NPC-aging connection. While intellectually interesting and logically coherent, these ideas (C160-C164) are entirely speculative without experimental support. They represent interesting frameworks for future investigation but are not supported by the current data.

results.result: Old yeast cells (18-22 CBE) lose chromosomes at a frequency of 10-15%, as demonstrated by fluorescent chromosome labeling. The loss is independent of labeling method or chromosome identity, affects entire chromosomes (not just labeled regions), is fatal to cells, and occurs specifically in the last division of old mother cells.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the findings are 'convincingly supported by carefully-designed experimental data.' Reviewer 3 describes the discovery as 'quite striking and well supported with solid experimental evidence' using 'classic microscopy-based single cell fluorescent chromosome assays that are appropriate and seem robust.' No concerns were raised about these core observations.

results.result: Chromosome loss in old cells occurs through asymmetric sister chromatid non-disjunction during anaphase, with 11% of anaphases showing co-segregation of sister chromatids to a single pole, and 82% of these missegregation events resulting in asymmetric partition to the bud. Non-disjoining chromatids remain attached to and co-segregate with the pre-existing (old) SPB.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this mechanistic finding. Reviewer 2 states the authors 'reveal that, in old yeast mother cells, chromosome loss occurs through asymmetric partitioning of chromosomes to daughter cells, a process coupled with the inheritance of an old Spindle Pole Body.' Reviewer 4 notes the authors 'first establish that aged mother cells exhibit aberrant error correction during mitosis.' No methodological concerns were raised about the anaphase analysis.

results.result: Old cells lose chromosomes due to defects in correcting syntelic chromosome attachment errors, as demonstrated by experiments with the temperature-sensitive ipl1-321 aurora B kinase mutant. The effects of age and reducing Ipl1 activity are non-additive, indicating they act through the same pathway.
results.evaluation: This mechanistic interpretation is accepted by reviewers. Reviewer 4 explicitly states the authors 'establish that aged mother cells exhibit aberrant error correction during mitosis' and describes the finding as 'compelling.' The ipl1-321 experiments are not questioned, and the non-additive effects support the proposed mechanism.

results.result: NPC remodeling and nuclear basket displacement trigger chromosome loss in aging cells. Genetic manipulations that increase ERC accumulation (sir2Δ) or destabilize the basket (mlp1Δ) promote premature chromosome loss, while interventions that prevent ERC accumulation (fob1Δ) or ERC anchorage to NPCs (sgf73Δ) suppress chromosome loss.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this causal connection. Reviewer 1 states the findings show 'aging in yeast leads to chromosome mis-segregation...driven by disruption of the nuclear pore complex.' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'identify that remodeling of the nuclear pore complex (NPC), specifically the displacement of its nuclear basket, triggers these asymmetric segregation events.' Reviewer 3 states 'the correlation of this phenotype with other age-associated phenotypes - specifically extrachromosomal rDNA circles and nuclear pore dysfunction - is supported by in vivo genetic manipulations.'

results.result: Removing the introns from three genes involved in chromosome segregation (NBL1, MCM21, GLC7) - which are the only intron-containing genes in the chromosome segregation machinery - nearly completely suppresses chromosome loss and anaphase missegregation in old cells, extends replicative lifespan by ~20%, and has no detectable effects in young cells.
results.evaluation: This is described as a key finding by all reviewers. Reviewer 2 states 'Through genetic manipulation, the study demonstrates that removing introns from key chromosome segregation genes is sufficient to prevent chromosome loss in aged cells.' Reviewer 4 calls this finding 'highly compelling' and notes 'the finding that deleting the introns of 3 genes in the Aurora B pathway can suppress age-related chromosome missegregation is highly compelling.' No concerns were raised about these experiments.

results.result: Young mlp1Δ mutant cells (lacking the nuclear basket protein) exhibit premature chromosome missegregation with similar characteristics to old wild-type cells (fourfold increase in missegregation, 80% following old SPB), and this phenotype is suppressed by removing the three introns, demonstrating that basket defects are sufficient to cause the aging phenotype.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as strong evidence for the causal role of basket displacement. Reviewer 4 notes 'The 3x∆i mutant also suppresses the increased chromosome loss resulting from nuclear basket destabilization in a mlp1∆ mutant.' The parallel between mlp1Δ and aging phenotypes strengthens the mechanistic model without raising reviewer concerns.

results.result: Old cells exhibit pre-mRNA leakage to the cytoplasm, as demonstrated by smRNA FISH showing ~70% of GLC7 intronic sequences in the cytoplasm of old cells (vs ~3% in young cells) and by a pre-mRNA translation reporter showing increased mCherry/GFP ratio in old cells. This leakage correlates with ERC accumulation (increased in sir2Δ, decreased in fob1Δ).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 2 states 'This disruption also leads to the leakage of unspliced pre-mRNAs into the cytoplasm, highlighting a breakdown in RNA quality control.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the application of the single cell mRNA splicing defect reporter showed very convincingly that general mRNA splicing is compromised in aged cells.' Reviewer 4 states the authors 'directly test if aged cells do exhibit aberrant mRNA export, using RNA FISH to identify that old cells indeed leak intron-containing pre-mRNA into the cytoplasm.'

results.result: Promoting pre-mRNA leakage in young cells (hrb1Δ gbp2Δ double mutant) is sufficient to induce asymmetric chromosome missegregation (>10-fold increase) that is biased toward the old SPB and suppressed by removing the three introns. In contrast, spliceosome defects (snu66Δ) cause missegregation without SPB bias, indicating the phenotype is due to pre-mRNA leakage rather than splicing defects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as strong evidence for sufficiency. Reviewer 2 states 'Moreover, promoting pre-mRNA leakage in young cells mimics the chromosome mis-segregation observed in old cells, providing further evidence for the critical role of nuclear envelope integrity and RNA processing in aging-related genome instability.' Reviewer 4 notes 'Mutants causing increased pre-mRNA leakage are sufficient to induce chromosome missegregation, which is suppressed by the 3x∆i.' The distinction from spliceosome mutants strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: Introducing an artificial DNA circle (YRp17) promotes premature chromosome loss and shortens lifespan, effects that are substantially (though not completely) suppressed by the 3x∆i mutations. Similarly, the 3x∆i mutations partially suppress the premature chromosome loss and shortened lifespan of sir2Δ mutant cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these experiments, which provide additional support for the model. The partial suppression is acknowledged in the manuscript and does not appear to concern reviewers, as it suggests both intron-dependent and intron-independent mechanisms can contribute to chromosome loss when ERC levels are very high.

results.result: The authors propose an integrated mechanistic model: ERC accumulation causes NPC basket displacement, leading to pre-mRNA leakage of intron-containing transcripts (NBL1, MCM21, GLC7), which impairs the aurora B error correction pathway, resulting in failed correction of syntelic attachments and asymmetric chromosome segregation. NPC remodeling is both necessary and sufficient to drive age-associated chromosome loss.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorse this integrated model. Reviewer 1 states the study 'reveals that aging in yeast leads to chromosome mis-segregation due to asymmetric partitioning of chromosomes, driven by disruption of the nuclear pore complex and pre-mRNA leakage' and that findings are 'convincingly supported.' Reviewer 2 describes the work as providing 'a compelling insight into the basis of chromosome missegregation in aged cells, tying this phenomenon to the established Nuclear Pore Complex architecture remodeling.' Reviewer 4 states the paper 'provides a compelling insight into the basis of chromosome missegregation in aged cells.'

results.result: Background claims about NPC remodeling in aging across species, yeast replicative aging, ERC biology, and the role of centromeres in chromosome segregation, all supported by citations to previous literature.
results.evaluation: These are established background facts cited from the literature. Reviewers do not question these foundational claims, which provide context for the novel findings. Reviewer 4 explicitly notes the work ties findings 'to the established Nuclear Pore Complex architecture remodeling that occurs with aging across a large span of diverse organisms.'

results.result: Speculative discussion about broader implications: basket displacement might affect other cellular processes beyond chromosome segregation (protein quality control, gene activation, mitochondrial function, ribosome assembly); the mechanism might be relevant to stress responses, cancer, progeria, and might represent an evolutionarily conserved response to pathogenic DNA.
results.evaluation: These are clearly presented as speculative implications in the Discussion section. Reviewers do not object to this speculation, which is appropriately framed as possibilities for future investigation rather than established conclusions. The speculation is grounded in the experimental findings and cited literature.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the finding that old yeast cells lose chromosomes while young cells retain them (C24-C32). OpenEval emphasizes the convergence of multiple labeling methods and dual-labeling controls. Peer reviewers describe the evidence as 'convincingly supported' and 'quite striking and well supported with solid experimental evidence.' Both also address centromere-dependent chromosome loss (C35, C37, C38), though peer review groups this with the core observation while OpenEval separates it into R2.

OpenEval R2 focuses specifically on centromere-dependent chromosome loss (C35-C38) with gain/loss-of-function experiments. Peer R1 includes some of these claims (C35, C37, C38) within their broader evaluation of chromosome loss observations. Both evaluations are supportive, with no disagreements on the evidence quality.

Both support the mechanism of chromosome missegregation through anaphase non-disjunction (C39-C42). OpenEval emphasizes the quantitative agreement between chromosome loss frequency and missegregation frequency. Peer reviewers affirm the finding that 'chromosome loss occurs through asymmetric partitioning' and note the coupling with old SPB inheritance. Both find the time-lapse microscopy evidence compelling.

Both support the SPB identity-dependent mechanism (C43-C46). OpenEval highlights the elegance of using SPB inheritance inversions as a natural experiment and the 80% co-segregation rate. Peer reviewers describe the process as 'coupled with the inheritance of an old Spindle Pole Body.' Both evaluations are aligned and supportive.

Perfect agreement on the error correction mechanism involving Ipl1/Aurora B (C47-C52). Both evaluations support the interpretation that aging affects the same pathway as reduced Ipl1 activity, based on non-additivity of effects. OpenEval notes the background knowledge is 'well-established and correctly applied,' while peer reviewers find the evidence 'compelling' with no methodological concerns raised.

Both strongly support the genetic evidence linking ERC levels to chromosome loss (C53-C60). OpenEval emphasizes the bidirectional manipulations (sir2Δ increasing ERCs, fob1Δ decreasing ERCs) with corresponding opposite effects. Peer reviewers affirm the 'correlation of this phenotype with...extrachromosomal rDNA circles and nuclear pore dysfunction' supported by 'in vivo genetic manipulations.' Both find the sgf73Δ evidence strengthens the NPC connection.

Both support the sufficiency of basket displacement to cause chromosome loss (C61-C62). OpenEval notes the mlp1Δ phenotype is 'strong and consistent' while acknowledging the mechanism remains unknown. Peer reviewers include this as part of the broader NPC disruption evidence. Both evaluations are aligned with no concerns raised.

Both strongly support the critical role of three specific introns in chromosome segregation genes (C63-C75). OpenEval provides detailed analysis of specificity evidence including tubulin intron controls and chromosome-independence. Peer reviewers describe the finding as 'highly compelling' and note it prevents chromosome loss in aged cells. Both emphasize the lifespan extension validates functional significance.

Perfect agreement that basket displacement in young cells (mlp1Δ) recapitulates the aging phenotype (C76-C82). Both note the similarity in SPB bias and suppression by intron removal. OpenEval emphasizes the partial lifespan rescue indicates intron-dependent effects are major but not sole contributors. Peer reviewers note the 3xΔi suppresses mlp1Δ-induced chromosome loss, strengthening the mechanistic model.

Both support that DNA circle accumulation (independent of ERCs) causes chromosome loss (C83-C87). OpenEval notes partial suppression by intron removal indicates both intron-dependent and intron-independent mechanisms. Peer reviewers accept these experiments without concerns, acknowledging the partial suppression pattern when ERC levels are very high.

Both support the genetic evidence linking DNA circles to intron-dependent chromosome loss (C88-C91). OpenEval notes the modest effect in sir2Δ background suggests additional mechanisms at very high ERC levels. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these experiments, which provide additional support for the model.

Both strongly support the direct visualization of pre-mRNA leakage in aged cells (C94-C98). OpenEval emphasizes the specificity controls and dramatic age-dependent change with 3/3 introns showing leakage. Peer reviewers describe the single-cell mRNA splicing reporter as showing 'very convincingly that general mRNA splicing is compromised in aged cells' and note RNA FISH confirms 'old cells indeed leak intron-containing pre-mRNA into the cytoplasm.'

Both support that leaked pre-mRNAs are translated in the cytoplasm (C99-C102). OpenEval notes the genetic manipulations affecting ERC levels show expected correlations. Peer reviewers affirm 'This disruption also leads to the leakage of unspliced pre-mRNAs into the cytoplasm, highlighting a breakdown in RNA quality control.' Both find the reporter design appropriate.

Both strongly support the critical distinction between pre-mRNA leakage and splicing defects (C105-C111). OpenEval emphasizes that hrb1Δ gbp2Δ recapitulates the aging phenotype while snu66Δ does not, demonstrating leakage rather than splicing per se causes the defect. Peer reviewers note 'Mutants causing increased pre-mRNA leakage are sufficient to induce chromosome missegregation, which is suppressed by the 3xΔi,' strengthening the interpretation.

Both support the main mechanistic pathway synthesis (C112-C115). OpenEval notes the causal chain is well-supported by convergent evidence and appropriately acknowledges the precise molecular mechanism remains unknown. Peer reviewers describe the work as providing 'a compelling insight into the basis of chromosome missegregation in aged cells' with findings 'convincingly supported.'

Both support the necessity and sufficiency evidence from genetic experiments (C116-C119). OpenEval emphasizes bidirectional manipulations provide strong support for causality. Peer reviewers explicitly endorse the integrated model, noting the work 'ties this phenomenon to the established Nuclear Pore Complex architecture remodeling.'

Both support the reasoning about specificity of the ERC-NPC connection (C120-C124). OpenEval notes the logic is sound: while individual mutations have multiple effects, their common denominator and independent confirmation by sgf73Δ support the mechanism. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about potential confounders, accepting the proposed specificity.

Both strongly support the comprehensive mechanistic summary (C125-C135). OpenEval emphasizes the key insight that intron removal separates aging from chromosome loss, establishing causality. Peer reviewers describe findings as 'convincingly supported' and providing 'compelling insight' with the model tying findings to 'established Nuclear Pore Complex architecture remodeling.' Both find the evidence strong and convergent.

Both recognize these claims (C136-C142) as speculative. OpenEval rates them as UNCERTAIN, noting they are 'largely speculative' based on known basket functions and intron distribution patterns without direct experimental support in this study. Peer reviewers accept the speculation as 'appropriately framed as possibilities for future investigation rather than established conclusions.' Both agree the speculation is reasonable but not experimentally demonstrated.

Both recognize these claims (C143-C150) as speculative extensions to stress response and cancer biology. OpenEval rates them as UNCERTAIN, noting cited evidence for basket displacement during stress is valid but evolutionary advantages and cancer relevance are 'speculative hypotheses without direct experimental support.' Peer reviewers 'do not object to this speculation' when clearly presented in the Discussion section. Both agree the speculation is grounded but not proven.

Both recognize these claims (C151-C157) as speculative extensions to mammalian systems. OpenEval rates them as UNCERTAIN, noting cited evidence for basket displacement in mammals is valid but functional relevance to mammalian aging and progeria 'remains speculative.' Peer reviewers accept this as appropriate Discussion content. Both agree the connection is not experimentally demonstrated but represents reasonable future directions.

Both recognize these claims (C158-C164) as highly speculative evolutionary hypotheses. OpenEval rates them as UNCERTAIN, describing them as 'entirely speculative without experimental support' but 'intellectually interesting and logically coherent.' Peer reviewers accept them as appropriately framed speculation. Both agree these represent interesting frameworks for future investigation but are not supported by current data.

Peer R11 addresses established background facts from the literature (C7-C23, C33-C34, C36) that provide context for the novel findings. OpenEval does not have a dedicated result for these background claims, as they are incorporated into other evaluations. Peer reviewers note these are 'established' facts not questioned in the review process.
